items.text: A DFS analyst writes: "This running back will likely bust this week, since his offensive line is banged up and the opposing defense ranks third against the run." Which sentence is the conclusion?

A. This running back will likely bust this week — The two "since"-flagged clauses are premises offered as reasons; the claim they support, that the back will likely bust, is the conclusion, even though it is stated first in the sentence.
"This contractor replaced forty roofs last year. He's the right guy for your job." There are no indicator words here. What is the correct way to tell whether this is actually an argument?

B. Check if inserting "therefore" between the two sentences preserves the meaning; if it does, it is an argument — Indicator words are a shortcut, not a requirement. Real arguments, especially pitches, often strip them out. Testing with an inserted "therefore" reveals the premise-conclusion structure either way.
A sales rep says: "Our dehumidifiers run around the clock in your basement, so your mold risk is zero." What is the unstated assumption the conclusion actually depends on?

C. That continuous dehumidification alone is sufficient to eliminate all mold risk, regardless of ventilation or hidden moisture — The premise, continuous dehumidification, only supports a strong claim like zero risk if you also assume dehumidification alone is sufficient for that outcome, with no role for ventilation, wall cavities, or already-contaminated material. That assumption is never stated and is too strong once said aloud.
A trader argues: "This stock gapped up on high volume at the open, so it's going higher today." What is the fastest way to expose the gap in this argument?

D. Ask what unstated assumption would have to be true for a volume-backed gap to guarantee the rest of the day continues the same direction, then check if that is actually true — Finding the assumption gap means naming exactly what unstated premise the conclusion depends on (that a volume-backed gap reliably continues through the day) and then testing it, rather than just disagreeing with the conclusion on vibes.
"If the water intrusion is Category 3, then all porous materials must be removed." A technician finds no porous materials removed on a job file. What can be validly concluded?

A. Nothing firm, unless "removal was not done" is actually established as true, not just a possibly incomplete file — The contrapositive of "if Category 3, then removal required" is "if removal not required (or not done), then not Category 3," which is valid, but only if "removal not done" is actually established, not merely that a file looks incomplete.
"If a loss is excluded under the policy, the carrier does not owe payment." What is the valid contrapositive of this statement?

B. If the carrier owes payment, the loss was not excluded — The contrapositive of "if A, then B" is "if not B, then not A." Here that is "if the carrier owes payment (not B), then the loss was not excluded (not A)," which is logically guaranteed.
"If the water is Category 3, then porous materials must be removed." A homeowner reasons: "removal was required here, so the water must have been Category 3." Which error is this?

C. The converse treated as if it were valid — This reasons from the consequent (removal required) back to the antecedent (Category 3 water), which is exactly the converse of the original statement, and the converse is not equivalent. A slow Category 1 leak with mold growth could also force removal.

A closer says: "If you sign the contract today, you lock in this quoted price." A homeowner hears this as, "so if I want to lock in this price, I have to sign today." What logical move did the homeowner just make?

D. Incorrectly swapped the statement for its converse — The homeowner treated "if A, then B" as if it also meant "if B, then A" (the converse), assuming signing today is the only way to lock the price, which the original statement never claimed.
"We will start mold remediation only if the moisture meter reads below 15 percent." With A = we start remediation and B = meter reads below 15 percent, which translation is correct?

A. If A, then B, because "only if" marks a necessary condition sitting on the consequent side — "A only if B" translates to "if A, then B." Verified by substitution: remediation actually starting (A) guarantees the threshold was already met (B), which matches "if A, then B" exactly.
"Unless the insured gives notice of loss within the policy's deadline, the claim is barred." With A = gives timely notice and B = claim is barred, which translation is correct?
B. If not A, then B — "Unless A, B" translates to "if not A, then B." The absence of timely notice is exactly what triggers the bar, matching the real meaning of the sentence.
"Being on the active NFL roster is necessary for a player to score fantasy points that week." With A = on the active roster and B = scores fantasy points, which translation correctly captures this?

C. If B, then A is correct, because scoring points guarantees the player was active, but being active does not guarantee scoring — "A is necessary for B" translates to "if B, then A." Substitution check: a player can be active and score zero (A true, B false), so "if A, then B" fails; but scoring any points absolutely requires active status, so "if B, then A" holds.
"Signing today is sufficient to lock in this quoted price." With A = sign today and B = price is locked, what does this statement NOT promise?

D. That signing today is the only way to lock the price — "Sufficient" only establishes "if A, then B." It never claims A is necessary for B, so it does not promise signing today is the only path to locking the price.

A carrier handbook says: "A supplemental estimate is reviewed only if it is submitted with photo documentation." A contractor submits photo documentation with his supplement. Can he validly conclude it will be reviewed?

A. No, because photo documentation is necessary for review, not sufficient; other requirements could still block review — "Reviewed only if photo documentation submitted" translates to "if reviewed, then documented," meaning documentation is necessary for review. Satisfying a necessary condition does not guarantee the outcome; other conditions could still be missing.

A policy states: "If a loss is caused by flood, then it is excluded from coverage." An adjuster observes a claim was denied as excluded and reasons: "this claim is excluded, so the loss must have been caused by flood." Name the fallacy.

B. Affirming the consequent — The adjuster reasoned from the consequent (excluded) to the antecedent (flood), which only works if the converse were valid. It is not: earth movement, wear and tear, and intentional acts are also excluded under the same policy, so exclusion alone does not prove flood.

"If a roof is more than 20 years old, the carrier requires a four-point inspection before binding coverage." A homeowner's roof is 12 years old. He concludes: "so the carrier will not require a four-point inspection." Name the fallacy.

C. Denying the antecedent; the carrier could require the inspection for an unrelated reason, like a prior claim or a coastal wind zone — This denies the antecedent (roof not over 20 years) and wrongly concludes the consequent is false (no inspection required). The stated rule says nothing about other underwriting reasons that could independently trigger the same inspection.

"If a stock beats earnings estimates, the shares typically pop at the open." This stock missed estimates. A trader concludes: "so the shares will not pop at the open." What is the realistic counterexample that exposes the error?

D. The shares could still pop on unrelated news, like a buyback announcement or a short squeeze, since missing estimates does not rule that out — This is denying the antecedent. The original conditional only promises a pop when estimates are beaten; it says nothing about what happens on a miss, so other catalysts can independently produce a pop.

"If a player is ruled out on the injury report, he scores zero fantasy points." A DFS player had argued in advance: "if he scores zero, he must have been ruled out." The player was active, not ruled out, and scored zero. What fallacy did the advance reasoning commit?

A. Affirming the consequent; the player was active but had a scoreless game — Concluding the antecedent (ruled out) from the consequent (zero points) is affirming the consequent. Here the counterexample is real: an active, healthy player had a scoreless game, showing the inference was never guaranteed.

A public adjuster tells a homeowner: "If the roof was damaged by wind, the carrier owes replacement cost. The carrier paid replacement cost, so the roof must have been wind damaged." What is wrong with this?

B. It is affirming the consequent, which rests on the broader fact that a conditional makes no promise about what follows when only the consequent, not the antecedent, is known to be true — This is affirming the consequent: other perils besides wind can also trigger replacement cost. The single underlying fact behind every trap in this domain is that "if A, then B" promises nothing about the case where only B, or only not-A, is known; it only guarantees the forward direction and its contrapositive.

A trading rule states: "A trade is sufficient to count toward pattern-day-trader status if it is a same-day round trip in a margin account." A trader makes no same-day round trip and concludes: "so none of my trades count toward that status." What is the error?

C. Denying the antecedent; "sufficient" only establishes "if A, then B," leaving open whether some other rule independently makes a different trade count — "Sufficient" translates only to "if A, then B," which says nothing about what happens when A is false. Concluding not-B from not-A is denying the antecedent; a different rule could independently trigger the same status.

A contract clause reads: "The warranty is honored if the homeowner keeps the gutters cleaned annually." With A = warranty honored and B = gutters cleaned annually, which translation is correct, and what can you NOT conclude if the gutters were not cleaned?

D. If B, then A, since plain "if" marks a sufficient condition for A; not cleaning the gutters does not by itself prove the warranty is void, since this clause never said cleaning was necessary — "A if B" translates to "if B, then A": cleaning the gutters is a sufficient condition for the warranty, not a necessary one (that would require "only if"). So the clause alone does not establish that skipping the cleaning voids the warranty.
